item.title: IDEA: A beginners guide to visiting Sitka, Alaska, by cruise ship
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Although not as popular as the “big three” Alaska ports — Ketchikan, Juneau and Skagway — Sitka is an adventure in its own right. Located on the rugged shores of Baranof Island, Sitka is attracting more cruise ships than ever before, thanks to its brand-new Sitka Sound Cruise Terminal that can accommodate up to two large ships at the same time. This quaint city is a nature-lover’s paradise. Home to the Alaska Raptor Center and the Fortress of the Bear, it provides insight into Alaska’s wildlife in a way that other ports of call can’t match. Sitka has something else that other ports in Southeast Alaska lack: a strong Russian history. The settlement was under Russian control from 1799 to 1867, when it was known as New Archangel. It was also here that the Alaska Purchase took place on October 18, 1867 – the date Russia was sold to the United States for $7.2 million. Today, Sitka offers a fascinating mix of Tlingit (pronounced kling-it) history, Russian influence and Americana that is unique in southeast Alaska. Combine that with its incredible nature, wildlife and scenery, and Sitka makes a great addition to any Alaska cruise itinerary. - It's home to some of Southeast Alaska’s only Russian-Orthodox architecture. - There is abundant nature at your fingertips. - The charming town has a large array of shops and restaurants. - The cruise pier is a distance from town, and shuttle wait times can be long during peak periods. While some small ships still anchor out in the bay and tender passengers into the heart of Sitka’s downtown, most cruise passengers will find themselves docked at the Sitka Sound Cruise Terminal, approximately 6 miles northwest of downtown Sitka. Complimentary shuttle buses whisk passengers into town, but when two ships are in port at the same time, lines can get lengthy. In fact, passengers must now reserve their shuttle to town in advance, though no reservations are required to return to the pier from Sitka. Upgrades to the new terminal were made in 2020 and 2021, and the updated facility boasts shops, restaurants, bars and information right at the pier. Passengers on shore excursions will get picked up from and returned to the cruise terminal, unless otherwise specified. Language: English is the official language in Sitka. Currency: The U.S. dollar is used for all purchases in Sitka. Time zone: Sitka is in the Alaska Time Zone (GMT-8), one hour behind Pacific Standard Time and four hours behind Eastern Standard Time. By far, the most popular things to do in Sitka revolve around nature. The Alaska Raptor Center is a fascinating rehabilitation, education and research center that is an easy 30-minute walk from downtown and is included on many Sitka shore excursions. If you go independently, plan to spend at least an hour here (maybe more if you're a birder or have bird-obsessed little ones in tow). The other heavy hitter in Sitka is the Fortress of the Bear, a rescue sanctuary for orphaned bears. Opened in 2007, the center’s mission is to care for bears orphaned as cubs, bring them back to health and provide the animals with long lives that may include eventual release into the wild in conjunction with the Alaska Department of Fish and Game. While you can visit independently, booking as part of a cruise line shore excursion is recommended due to extensive entry wait times, particularly on busy ship days. Kayaking is also a popular pastime in Sitka, thanks to the pristine waters that run near the city and its outer islands. If you’re into outdoor adventures, Sitka is the place you want to seriously consider for a more active excursion. There’s an abundance of fantastic shore excursions to participate in here, from wildlife viewing to kayaking to fly fishing, rafting and even guided hikes. Siginaka Islands cruise and kayak adventure This 90-minute kayak session offers the chance to see ocean wildlife up close from the comfort of ocean kayaks that can seat two people. The Siginaka Islands make the perfect location for this adventure, with numerous narrow passages and calm ocean currents, that allow you to easily drift or paddle along and enjoy the sights. Cruise lines offer a number of different excursions to the Fortress of the Bear, which is, on many Alaska cruises, the only guaranteed opportunity to see bears. These trips to the Fortress of the Bear rehabilitation center sell out on nearly every cruise, so booking in advance is essential. Alaska Raptor Center and cultural discovery Like Fortress of the Bear, trips to the Alaska Raptor Center are some of the first shore excursions to fill up Popular with families, this excursion typically also includes a panoramic drive, a guided visit to the Alaska Raptor Center and a cultural performance by the Alaska Storyteller Dancers. One of several excursions that include a visit to Fin Island Lodge in Sitka Sound, this tour is popular for its wildlife cruise, which offers a chance to see whales, sea otters or even distant brown bears. Coming ashore at the lodge, guests can walk the shoreline or sit by the fire before enjoying a meal of Alaskan crab, freshly caught fish, prime rib and dessert before returning on their tour boat to the cruise pier. - On foot: Once the cruise shuttle drops you in town, you can easily explore much of downtown on foot. - Taxi: While taxi services are available in Sitka, they can be difficult to find without booking in advance. Use the cruise ship shuttle to take you into downtown, or book an excursion if you’re interested in venturing farther out. - Bike or scooter: A handful of bike and e-bike rental shops are available in Sitka should you want to venture further afield. - Car: Car rentals are not widely available in Sitka. And truly, there’s no need for one, anyhow. While there are plenty of restaurants located in downtown Sitka, there are also a handful of good options located at the Sitka Sound Cruise Terminal. These include Halibut Point Crab and Chowder, which sells locally sourced Dungeness crab, and the Wheelhouse Pub, serving up cold Alaskan brews alongside pub-style Alaskan food and seafood. In town, the Bayview Pub on Lincoln Street is a long-standing favorite that overlooks the inner harbor and serves up solid pub-style food and plenty of local beers. Mean Queen on Harbor Drive also overlooks Sitka’s inner harbor and serves a huge menu of favorites, and they're open from 8 a.m. until 2 a.m. every day. Some of the best pizza we’ve ever eaten has been at Harbor Mountain Brewing Company. It’s about a 30-minute walk from downtown, past the Sitka National Historic Park, and has a Campfire Kitchen Pizza tucked away within it. Order a pint and give yourself some time, these pizzas take time but are worth the wait. For an authentic Alaskan bar experience, hit up the Pioneer Bar on Katlian Street, just past the Sitka Pioneer Home. It’s not as rough as it appears, and it's popular with both locals and tourists alike. When in Alaska, the word of the day is seafood. Ask if anything is locally caught or in season; seafood or salmon chowders are always an excellent choice in Sitka, as is crab. Locally brewed beers are an excellent choice to pair with any meal. It’s also tough to go wrong with burgers and pizza. You can pop by Sitka Pel’Meni for a taste of Russian cuisine that reflects the town’s long Russian history that is also wholly unique within Alaska. All your shopping needs are catered to in Downtown Sitka, with stores that range from large multinational corporations to local, independently run shops. So while you’ll find the likes of Diamonds International in Sitka — ubiquitous across Alaska — you’ll also find local wares, too. Shops are typically found on and near Lincoln Street, which runs the length of downtown. These include fine art galleries, stores specializing in local Tlingit culture and gift shops that offer standard goods like T-shirts, salmon, Ulu knives and other wares. Sitka does have a fantastic bookstore, Old Harbor Books, on Lincoln Street with a fabulous local interest section, while more practical shops like Russell’s (also on Lincoln) offer outdoor gear for those who may need to upgrade their outerwear for Alaska’s liquid sunshine. Although cruise lines offer excursions that explore the pristine forest of the Sitka National Historical Park, there’s no reason you can’t visit on your own. Located about 20 minutes from downtown, a leisurely stroll takes you into the heart of the park, which includes the Visitor Center and a Tlingit totem pole. It’s also entirely free to walk around downtown and take in the sights, such as the Russian Bishop’s House, St. Michael the Archangel Orthodox Cathedral and Baranof Castle State Historic Site. Families will want to hit up the excellent Community Kid’s Playground on Lincoln Street. It's about 10 minutes’ stroll past the Russian Bishop’s House, next door to the Sitka Sound Science Center. Sitka is an excellent port of call that offers some spectacular excursion options you won’t see elsewhere in Alaska. While the cruise pier is a distance from town, proper planning can make your day here one to remember.

item.title: REPORTING: Everything That Happens to Your Body on a Road Trip
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
Prepping for long road trips can feel exhilarating. Packed bags and itinerary set. Check. Salty, sweet snacks stashed in a handy spot? Check. Plush interior, blankets and pillows, blasting A/C, and a carefully curated cruising playlist ready? Check, check, check, and check. Of course, even the coziest upholstery and upbeat bangers can’t always shake that aching, exhausted feeling that sets in after the third or fourth hour on the road to your favorite trailhead or camping grounds. You’re not lifting heavy things or solving complex math equations in the car: you’re just sitting there. Why do long road trips make us feel so utterly blegh? Basically, a whole lot of nothing and everything is happening simultaneously when you’re stuck on the car for hours. “The human brain requires a certain level of stimulation to remain engaged and alert,” John Gaspar, PhD, told Outside. “Both too much and too little stimulation can lead to impaired performance.” Gaspar is the director of human factors research at the Driving Safety Research Institute at the University of Iowa. His main area of expertise is studying how humans interact with vehicles and how impairment, distraction, and other factors affect driving ability; one of his current projects focuses on alleviating drowsiness during long overnight drives. If you can relate to feeling pretty terrible during a long drive on your way to your ultimate outdoor destination, experts explain why and exactly what happens to your body on a road trip. Reading a book or doomscrolling for hours on end is a piece of cake. But focusing on the road for extended periods, however, is a totally different ballgame, Gaspar told Outside. “A driver’s eyes are really informative during fatigue– or drowsiness-impacted long drives,” Gaspar said. Even early in a road trip, drivers start to shift in their seats and do what they can to stay awake. This describes that antsy feeling you get while sitting in the driver’s seat. People may amp up the music volume or blast the A/C, Gaspar said. “At later stages in the drive, drivers will start having microsleep events, where they actually fall asleep for several seconds. These changes happen pretty quickly, especially when drivers are somewhat sleep-deprived,” he said. These microsleeps, Gaspar explained, can occur within the first hour to 90 minutes of a long drive. Unfortunately, he says the things you might do to wake yourself up—like rolling down your window or cranking up the music—are virtually useless in regaining alertness. “People do a lot of things they think will help with fatigue that have actually been shown to have little to no benefit,” he explained. In short, Gaspar said, sitting in the car for a long period feels bad and tiring because you’re understimulated and overstimulated at the same time. You might feel overtaxed by the stress of navigating and swerving around angry jerks in suped-up monster trucks, but simultaneously understimulated from moving down a long stretch of road, he said. Together, they’re a bad combination for staying alert. According to Brian M. Cervoni Rosario, MD, a sports medicine physiatrist at Boston Medical Center, your upper body can take a beating during long hauls on the road. “The neck and shoulders suffer disproportionately because drivers actively stabilize the head against vehicle motion while maintaining forward gaze, creating sustained isometric contraction (tightening of the muscle) in the neck flexors and upper trapezius,” Dr. Rosario told Outside. In other words, your neck and upper back muscles get really strained. Plus, if weaving through traffic stresses you out (which is probably the case for all of us), you might carry a ton of that tension in your neck and shoulders, hence the stiff upper body. Gripping and controlling the wheel for an extended period can affect your hands, too. A 2022 study of taxi drivers found that their handgrip decreases because of the car’s vibration while it’s being operated. For a lot of us, driving feels like second nature—the average American spends about one hour behind the wheel daily, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA) Foundation for Traffic Safety. Given how frequently we cruise, it’s sometimes easy to forget we’re operating a 4,000-pound piece of heavy, complex machinery, one with near-constant movement and vibrations. Those same vibrations that affect grip strength pulse through the entire body, too, affecting your driving and contributing to pain. “Vibration transmission from the vehicle seat amplifies spinal loading, particularly at the lumbar and cervical regions,” Dr. Rosario said. The cervical region of the spine includes the seven vertebrae of the neck that support your head. Plus, your lower body also undergoes subtle but repetitive isometric muscle contractions to reach and press the pedals with your legs and feet, which research shows can often lead to discomfort over time. Sitting for long periods also places a significant amount of compression on the butt, thighs, and back, resulting in stiffness. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention notes that people who sit in vehicles for prolonged periods are more likely to develop blood clots, so it’s especially important to get out and move whenever you can. Predictability is crucial for a healthy stomach, Rudolph Bedford, MD, a board-certified gastroenterologist at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, California, told Outside. But on a road trip, your routine can get wildly out of whack. “When you move, your gut moves. You don’t move, it doesn’t move, so when you’re sitting in a car for long periods, you can get backed up,” he said. “Bloating and gassiness are very typical of bus drivers and cab drivers; they’re traveling a lot. The constipation is a setup for hemorrhoids to occur.” He said a seatbelt compressing on your stomach doesn’t help much, either. What’s more, you’re probably not grabbing the most gut-friendly items—like a fiber-packed apple or a pack of carrots—at whatever gas station, fast-food restaurant, or questionable local dive bar you find on the road. “Usually people are reaching for foods that are low in fiber, high in fat, and have plenty of salt. All of those things tend to slow gastric emptying,” Dr. Bedford said, adding that sodas, sugar-free gums, and caffeine can also contribute to abdominal woes. For most of the ailments above, the primary, no-fail solution is to simply pull over. “Once fatigue and drowsiness set in, the best thing a driver can do is stop to rest, even if just for ten to 20 minutes,” Gaspar said. To alleviate abdominal discomfort: “Stop every two to three hours,” Dr. Bedford said. “Walk around for five to ten minutes just to keep things moving. It stimulates the bowels and keeps gas moving through your system. More importantly, it supports leg circulation.” If you don’t feel safe exiting your car, simply pulling over to twist your torso, flex your ankles, and focus on something besides the road can help. Yes, frequent pull-overs will make your ride longer. But as the trite old saying goes, those pit stops might make the journey feel like half the fun—or at least make the next part of the trip a bit less excruciating. Want more Outside health stories? Sign up for the Bodywork newsletter. And for tips on how to train, fuel, and recover better, sign up for the Sweat Science 101 newsletter.

item.title: IDEA: Clocks going back: how the time change affects UK travel
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
It's that time of the year again: this weekend (Sunday 25 October 2026) the clocks will change as the UK returns to Greenwich Mean Time. Long and light summer evenings have made way to cosy and dark evenings and afternoons as winter looms ever near. The time change can also have a surprising impact on our travel plans. Here's everything you need to know ahead of the change. When do the clocks change? The clocks change on Sunday 25 October at 1am. Are the clocks going forward or backwards? The clocks are ‘falling’ back – which means at 2am on Sunday, it becomes 1am again. We gain an hour of sleep to make up for the change. So on Sunday evening in London, the sun will set at around 4.50 pm vs 6.30pm on Saturday evening. How does the time change impact travel? Essentially, 2am becomes 1am again. That means that overnight bus, coach and train schedules might be impacted, with many services choosing to run twice during the hours that clocks go back. For example, a coach that normally leaves at 1.30am BST could also provide an additional service that leaves at 1.30am GMT an hour later. On a more basic level, the clocks changing results in an hour more sleep – meaning you might be more spritely and ready for that early morning transport. It's also important to make sure manual clocks (like alarm clocks or watches) are adjusted before you go to sleep on Saturday night, if you're relying on these to wake you up for something important on Sunday morning. Phone clocks will change automatically, so that's one less thing to think about. How does the time change work on flights? Here's where it feels extra confusing – when the clocks change while you're already crossing time zones. To add a little extra spice: not all countries change their clocks at the same time, or at all. - Popular tourist destinations like India, Japan, South Africa, Brazil and Turkey don't observe Daylight Saving Time, so their clocks remain the same year-round. - The USA changes back from Daylight Savings Time a week after the UK, so this year that'll be Sunday 1 November. - Most European countries change at the same time as the UK. So if you're flying overnight on Saturday evening/Sunday morning – for example, to India – the flight will seem an hour longer. Of course, you're in the air for the same amount of time, but the time difference has become one hour less; you may feel like you’ve landed earlier than expected, because the time difference has shrunk by an hour, even though the flight duration hasn’t changed. Airlines always display departure and arrival times in local time, so your ticket will be correct. Our advice? Change your watch to local time for your arrival destination when you board, so you don't have to think about the clocks changing at all. This helps with jet lag too.

item.title: REVIEW: Atmos Rewards Ascent Visa Signature review: Valuable points and solid perks for Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines flyers
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Editorial note: This is a recurring post, regularly updated with new information and offers. The may be the entry-level card option for Atmos Rewards, but it's anything but basic. This card packs a punch with a free checked bag and preferred boarding on Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines flights, with a fan-favorite $99 Companion Fare for cardholders who meet the spending requirements. Even if you don't fly Alaska or Hawaiian often, the points you earn on the card can help you get outsized value. With a robust network of Oneworld and nonalliance partners, Atmos Rewards can take you just about anywhere in the world. Card rating*: ⭐⭐⭐⭐ *Card rating is based on the opinion of TPG's editors and is not influenced by the card issuer. The is a cobranded airline card within Atmos Rewards, the joint loyalty program between Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines. For a $95 annual fee, the card earns valuable Atmos Rewards points and provides a few added benefits. Some of the best ways to maximize these points include redeeming for premium cabins with Oneworld partners, such as Cathay Pacific and Fiji Airways. However, Atmos Rewards points are also solid for short-haul domestic routes on Alaska Airlines and American Airlines. One of the card's standout perks is its annual $99 Companion Fare (plus taxes and fees from $23) that is earned each account anniversary as long as you've spent $6,000 or more in the prior anniversary year. Generally, it's a solid option for Alaska Airlines or Hawaiian Airlines frequent flyers, thanks to the perks provided when flying with either airline, such as free checked bags and preferred boarding. However, if you're looking for more premium perks like lounge access, this card won't meet your needs. The offers fewer benefits than other cobranded airline cards. However, you can still expect some perks. Perks when flying Alaska Airlines or Hawaiian Airlines Cardholders receive one piece of free checked luggage for themselves and up to six other passengers on the same reservation when flying Alaska or Hawaiian and paying with the Atmos Rewards Ascent. This saves at least $30 per person each way on checked bags, which is a significant savings if you fly with either airline frequently. Cardholders also get preferred boarding on Alaska and Hawaiian, and they'll receive 20% back on inflight purchases with both airlines when they use the card. If you're working toward Atmos Rewards status, you can earn 1 status point for every $3 spent on the card, with no cap on the number of status points you can earn through spending. As mentioned above, one of the best benefits of the Atmos Rewards Ascent is the $99 Companion Fare (plus taxes and fees from $23). This can be unlocked after spending $6,000 or more on the card within the prior anniversary year. You'll get value from this perk as long as you fly Alaska Airlines or Hawaiian Airlines with a friend or family member on paid fares at least once a year. Carly Helfand, TPG's director of content strategy, previously used the Ascent's Companion Fare to take a last-minute trip to Chicago with her husband. The round-trip flights from Portland International Airport (PDX) in Oregon to Chicago's O'Hare International Airport (ORD) cost $542.60 per person, but she paid $679.63 for both tickets thanks to the Companion Fare. While the Atmos Rewards Ascent doesn't provide outright lounge access, you can get $100 off an annual Alaska Lounge+ membership when you pay with this card. A membership costs $795 per year. This benefit alone offsets the card's $95 annual fee. However, given how expensive membership is, this perk isn't too useful unless you were already going to pay for an Alaska Lounge+ membership. It's worth noting that this card doesn't provide basic travel protections like baggage delay insurance, lost luggage insurance, purchase protection and trip cancellation/interruption coverage. If these perks are important to you, you may want to consider an alternative option. On a more positive note, this is a good card to take abroad since it doesn't charge foreign transaction fees. How to earn and use Atmos Rewards points The earns Atmos Rewards points on purchases. These points are often best redeemed toward air travel. Let's dive into what to know. With this card, you'll earn: - 3 points per dollar spent on eligible Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines purchases - 2 points per dollar spent on cable, at electric vehicle charging and gas stations, on local transit and ride-hailing services, and on select streaming services - 1 point per dollar spent on all other eligible purchases Plus, cardholders with an eligible Bank of America account will also receive a 10% bonus on all points earned from purchases. TPG's October 2026 valuations estimate Atmos Rewards points are worth 1.55 cents apiece. This card may not be the best option for spending categories outside of Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines purchases. However, if you're all in on earning Atmos Rewards points, swiping this card becomes more attractive. Atmos Rewards provides stellar redemption rates on domestic travel. Short-haul economy tickets start at just 4,500 points one-way. One of my favorite ways to redeem Atmos Rewards points is to book short-haul American Airlines flights, such as Charlotte Douglas International Airport (CLT) to Louisville Muhammad Ali International Airport (SDF) in Kentucky, at this 4,500-point rate. It can also be a good deal to redeem for longer domestic flights. For example, a one-way flight from Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA) to New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) starts at 12,500 points in economy. Premium cabins can start as low as 15,000 points one-way on shorter flights and 30,000 points one-way on longer U.S. routes. For trips to Hawaii, awards from the West Coast typically start at 12,500 points each way in economy and 30,000 points each way in first class. Atmos Rewards is part of the Oneworld alliance, which means you can book partner flights with airlines such as British Airways, Cathay Pacific and Qantas. Keep in mind that partner awards include a $20 nonrefundable booking fee. TPG director of travel content Eric Rosen's favorite ways to maximize Atmos Rewards redemptions include booking Cathay Pacific or Japan Airlines business class from the U.S. to Asia for 75,000 points one-way and Fiji Airways business class from the U.S. to Fiji for 75,000 points one-way. Where the Atmos Rewards Ascent falls short Despite its benefits, there are a few reasons why you may not want to apply to the $95-annual-fee : - The card does not include travel protections. - The card's earning rates aren't particularly high, and many other travel cards provide a better return for your spending. - You have to spend $6,000 on the card in an account anniversary year to earn the Companion Fare. - You must fly on Alaska Airlines or Hawaiian Airlines to receive a free checked bag or preferred boarding. Atmos Rewards Ascent vs. Atmos Rewards Summit If you are ready to go all in on Atmos Rewards, consider its premium sibling: the . For a higher $395 annual fee, the card provides Alaska Lounge passes, a 25,000-point Global Companion Award every year and a high earning rate on foreign purchases. Is the Atmos Rewards Ascent worth it? The is a great way to collect valuable Atmos Rewards points. If you value that currency highly, this card is a fantastic starting point. However, if you find the earning rates restrictive and the benefits underwhelming, another option may be the best choice. When to apply for the Atmos Rewards Ascent New cardholders can earn up to 80,000 bonus points and a $99 Companion Fare: Earn 60,000 bonus points and a $99 Companion Fare (plus taxes and fees from $23) after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first 90 days from account opening. Earn an additional 20,000 bonus points after spending a total of $5,000 on purchases, also in the first 90 days from account opening. Cardholders who meet the higher spending requirement will earn a total of 80,000 bonus Atmos Rewards points, which TPG values at $1,240. This is one of the highest bonus amounts we've seen in the card's offer history, making it a fantastic time to apply if you can earn the full bonus. Other cards to consider if you don't want the Atmos Rewards Ascent If you aren't certain about the , here are some alternatives worth considering: - If you want to earn Chase points: Go for the (see rates and fees), one of the top mid-tier travel cards on the market. It offers generous point-earning opportunities, especially on dining and streaming. These valuable points can be transferred to airline and hotel partners or redeemed directly for travel through Chase Travel℠. To learn more, read our full review of the Sapphire Preferred. - If you're after Capital One miles: The Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card combines fixed-value redemptions with 15-plus airline and hotel transfer partners. With its reasonable annual fee and attractive rewards on everyday spending, this card is a valuable asset worth holding onto. To learn more, read our full review of the Venture Rewards. - If you'd consider a business card: The has comparable benefits to the Atmos Rewards Ascent and is a solid option for business owners who frequently fly Alaska Airlines or Hawaiian Airlines. To learn more, read our full review of the Atmos Rewards Business. For additional options, check out our full list of the best travel credit cards. The Atmos Rewards points you'll earn on the unlock fantastic redemption rates on domestic flights, as well as international routes through its Oneworld partners. Award-savvy travelers know you don't have to be an Alaska Airlines or Hawaiian Airlines loyalist to enjoy the rewards you earn with this card. However, some of the card's perks may go unused if you don't at least occasionally fly with one of its primary airlines. Consider what matters most to you in exchange for a $95 annual fee, and you'll be on your way to hitting the skies.

item.title: INSTRUCTION: Alton Brown's Brined Turkey
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
If youâre wondering how to fit an enormous brine-bathing bird into your fridge this holiday season, stop wondering. Alton Brownâs wet-brined turkey recipe uses an insulated cooler instead, freeing up precious refrigerator space while seasoning the bird throughout. The brineâa simple mixture of kosher salt, sugar, and vegetable brothâhelps the turkey retain moisture as it roasts. Once the bird has had its soak, pat it thoroughly dry and send it into a blazing-hot 500Â°F oven to get the skin hurtling toward golden and crisp. After 30â40 minutes, youâll shield the breast with foil, lower the heat to 350Â°F, and let the turkey finish roasting. Thatâs right: No basting. No hovering by the oven. Just a little advance planning and plenty of time to focus on sweet potatoes, apple pie, and the rest of your Thanksgiving feast. If you'd rather skip the wet brine, try our dry-brined turkey. Short on time? Chris Moroccoâs turkey in parts cooks in under two hours. How long should you brine a turkey? For a 14â18-lb. turkey, plan on 8â12 hours in the brineâenough time for the salt to work its way into the meat, seasoning it and helping it retain moisture. You may be tempted to leave the turkey soaking for 24 hours, but an extended brine can make it overly salty. Stick to the recommended window. Is brining turkey in a cooler safe? Yes, as long as you can keep the brine at or below 40Â°F the entire time. Use a thoroughly cleaned, food-safe insulated cooler and monitor the liquid with a probe thermometer. Add sealed ice packs as needed to maintain a safe temperature. The goal is to keep the turkey just as cold as it would be in the refrigerator. Can you brine a turkey thatâs already been brined? Itâs best not to. Many supermarket turkeys are sold prebrined or injected with a salt solution, sometimes labeled âself-basting,â âenhanced,â or âcontains a solution.â Brining one again can make the meat too salty. Check the packaging before you begin and choose an unbrined turkey for this recipe. How do you keep gravy made from brined turkey from getting too salty? Brining seasons the turkey, but it can also make the pan drippings quite salty. Taste the gravy before adding any extra seasoning, and use low-sodium or unsalted broth for more control. If the finished gravy is too salty, add a few pats of unsalted butter or thin the gravy with salt-free broth. - All-Clad Roasting Pan With Rack $200 $132 At Amazon - Diamond Crystal Kosher Salt, 3 Pounds $11 At Amazon Need to make a substitution? - Turkey and BrineStep 1Place wrapped one 14â18-lb. Frozen turkey in a 5-gal. cooler with a drain spout. Place cooler in a bathtub and pour in cold water to cover turkey. Let sit, draining and replacing water every 2â3 hours and making sure to keep water temperature below 40Â°, until turkey is thawed, 8â10 hours. Step 2Remove turkey and clean cooler with soap and pat dry. Pour in 3 cups (1 lb.) Diamond Crystal or 1Â¾ cups Morton kosher salt, â cup sugar, and 2 qt. hot tap water. Stir to dissolve salt and sugar. Pour in 4 qt. low-sodium vegetable broth and 8 lb. ice (from 1 gallon water). Step 3Unwrap turkey and remove giblets and any other parts (such as neck) that may be inside cavity; save for gravy if desired. Place turkey, breast side up, in brine. If turkey floats, fill a 1-gallon resealable plastic bag with ice water and place it on top of turkey. Close lid and set cooler in a cool place. Let sit, turning turkey over once if possible, 8â12 hours. Check brining liquid periodically with a probe-style thermometer ; if temperature is above 40Â°, add a few freezer packs enclosed in resealable plastic bags. Step 4Place a rack in lower third of oven and remove remaining racks; preheat to 500Â°. Remove turkey from brine and pat dry inside and out with paper towels. Fill turkey cavity with 1 large onion, coarsely chopped, 2 large carrots, scrubbed, coarsely chopped, 2 celery stalks, coarsely chopped, and some thyme, rosemary, and/or sage sprigs; keep packing loose. Step 5Place turkey, breast side up, on a V-shaped rack set inside a large roasting pan. Cut a piece of foil big enough to cover breast and mold over breast. Remove foil, then coat foil with nonstick vegetable oil spray and set aside. Step 6Rub 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter between your hands until liberally coated (you may use disposable food-grade gloves if desired). Rub butter all over turkey, re-buttering your hands and repeating process until you have a nice, even coating. Step 7Slide turkey into oven neck end first and roast until well browned, 30â40 minutes. Remove turkey from oven and place greased foil over breast. Insert probe-style thermometer through foil into thickest part of breast. Reduce oven temperature to 350Â° and return turkey to oven. Roast until probe inserted into breast registers 161Â°, and 181Â° for thigh, 2â2Â½ hours (do not open oven to baste turkey). Step 8Transfer turkey to carving board and let rest 30 minutes. Reserve drippings for gravy. - Gravy and AssemblyStep 9Set roasting pan across 2 burners over medium heat. Add 1 cup low-sodium chicken broth and whisk to scrape up pan drippings. Whisk 1 Tbsp. cornstarch and 1 cup cold water in a small bowl to combine. Add cornstarch slurry to pan and cook, whisking, until gravy is glossy and thickened. Taste and season with kosher salt and freshly ground pepper if needed. Editorâs note: We first published this wet-brined turkey recipe in November 2011; it has been updated for style. If you and your guests havenât finished the whole bird by the nightâs end, put it to work in these leftover turkey recipes.

item.title: REPORTING: 19 People Have Been Rescued on Mount Shasta. Why Is the 14er So Dangerous?
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
Shasta-Trinity climbing ranger Christian Jordan ascending on the Whitney Glacier during the October 18 rescue operation (Photo: Courtesy of Nick Meyers/USFS) A flurry of rescues on California’s Mount Shasta this year has prompted officials to remind hikers that the popular 14,179-foot peak is also dangerous and potentially deadly. On October 18, a 39-year-old Florida man summited Whitney Glacier, a technical alpine climb accessible via Mount Shasta’s popular Avalanche Gulch route. During his downclimb, a snowbridge collapsed under his weight. He injured his leg, fell into a crevasse, and spent two days waiting for rescuers. The climber did not bring snow and ice equipment and wore sweatpants and a hoodie, according to the Mount Shasta Avalanche Center. Eventually, rescuers airlifted him to safety after he spent two nights at 12,000 feet. Siskiyou County Sheriff’s Office (SCSO) told Outside that it’s the 19th rescue on the mountain this year. Most of those rescued in 2026 had several things in common: they were young, underprepared, left the trailhead too late, and underestimated the challenge, according to SCSO spokesperson Sage Milestone. “We have seen this year that nearly every SAR incident began with someone failing to adhere to the noon turnaround rule,” Milestone told Outside. The rule Milestone is referring to is simple: climbers should turn around if they haven’t reached the Shasta summit by noon. On October 12, two hikers, 19 and 20, were lost on the mountain for 36 hours before officials located and rescued them. In September, a San Jose climber summited around 7:30 P.M.—seven hours past the recommended turn-around time—then slid 500 feet and crawled through the night on injured feet. A 71-year-old woman spent nearly a week lost in the Mount Shasta wilderness in late September, and in August, three men summited at 7 P.M., wandered off route in the dark, and spent the night stranded on the mountain. One later told sheriffs the duo used AI to plan their route, and the advice turned out to be drastically incorrect. There’s no cap on how many people can climb Mount Shasta each year. According to the U.S. Forest Service (USFS), between 5,000 and 6,000 people attempt the summit, and only about half reach the top. Mount Shasta’s reputation as an easier peak for mountaineering may be part of the problem, Milestone said. It sits about a 20-minute drive from the nearest highway, making it one of California’s more geographically accessible mountains over 14,000 feet. The Avalanche Gulch trailhead is just 12 miles from the town of Mount Shasta. It’s a non-technical route, though it gains approximately 7,000 feet of elevation. Novice mountaineers often flock to the peak because the route to the top includes ice, snow, and rock for much of the year. “Our theory at Siskiyou County Search and Rescue is that folks are becoming more aware of the mountain through social media and hear it described as a ‘beginner 14er,’ which is a misconception that we are trying to correct through public outreach and education,” Milestone said. You need specialty mountaineering gear to ascend the peak. The Forest Service advises climbers on the Avalanche Gulch route to bring crampons, ice axes, and a safety helmet, plus flashlights, extra food, and warm clothing. She also points to a growing trend in backcountry planning: relying on AI to plan and research routes without fact-checking or verifying against official sources. “I do know that the Forest Service climbing rangers have heard from more climbers that they are increasingly using AI to plan trips, or in some cases generate unique (and incorrect) maps of routes up Mount Shasta,” Milestone said. When Outside asked Google Gemini AI whether Mount Shasta is considered a beginner mountain, for example, it responded: “Mount Shasta is widely considered one of the best beginner mountaineering peaks in North America, but it is not a simple walkup or beginner hike.” However, the difficulty depends greatly on the time of year. Avalanche Gulch is a great option for reliable conditions in late spring and early summer, Milestone said, but conditions deteriorate by July, and informed climbers generally use other routes. Most climbers attempting a late-season summit are unfamiliar with the mountain or new to climbing. As snow melts, footing gets less reliable, and rockfall becomes a bigger risk, according to the Mount Shasta Avalanche Center. Guides follow the snow rather than a fixed calendar, Logan Talbott, a Shasta guide at Alpenglow Expeditions, told Outside. His company stops guiding once the snow melts and trails lose decent snow coverage, usually around August. “Conditions are rough right now: very little snowpack, and we’re at the very end of the season before the winter snow starts falling,” Talbott said. These conditions add risk as “things get dustier and looser,” increasing the chance of rockfalls. But in 2026, climbers were still heading up in October, more than three months after guides stopped operating. So many rescues in such a short time that the Mount Shasta Avalanche Center advised visitors to avoid parts of Avalanche Gulch. Milestone said that pleasant weather may be tempting people. “One unique attribute about this late summer-fall season is that the warmer, milder weather has persisted late into October, which could be encouraging more folks to climb later in the season than they normally could,” she said. That’s a stark contrast from 2025, when two climbers died in what she called “navigation issues due to the earlier onset of winter storms.” USFS data shows 11 search-and-rescue incidents on Mount Shasta in 2022, 10 in 2023, 9 in 2024, and 12 in 2025, including two fatalities. According to Milestone, it’s not just the sheer number of rescues that’s unusual, but also their timing. “We don’t usually have so many rescues this late in the year,” she said. Milestone’s theory is that climbers arrive at trailheads less prepared. “Most often folks think they can treat Mount Shasta—and Avalanche Gulch in particular—as a day hike.” In 2025, for example, USFS said most rescued were men between 30 and 50 with intermediate experience. Michael St. John leads the Marin County Sheriff’s Search and Rescue Team and responds to SAR calls across California, including multiple times in Shasta. Serious rescues on Shasta usually occur once or twice a year. “I haven’t seen Shasta be this busy,” he told Outside. Climbers increasingly rely on technology to navigate and call for help, but in several recent rescues, that technology proved unreliable. The San Jose climber’s phone died at the summit, and the two hikers stranded on October 12 lost theirs after calling for help. Milestone said that’s a pattern: rescuers often find people who became lost because their phones died. “Rarely are folks in these situations equipped with a physical map or alternate GPS device,” Milestone told Outside, “which again, speaks to their level of overall preparedness.” St. John says that technology works, but only when someone knows how to use it properly. “Overall, technology is more of an asset,” he said. But a phone can give people “extra confidence,” and many “just have a societal expectation that you can get 911 anywhere today.” Experts agree that these rescues shouldn’t deter people from getting into the backcountry; instead, they should remind climbers that a little preparedness can go a long way.

item.title: IDEA: I’ve Spent Years Tracking Nordic Wellness Trends, and This Low-Impact Finnish Ritual Is About to Take Over
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
I can smell the embers of a Nordic trend in the making from miles away. After all, even before the Swedish ethos of lagom (optimal balance) captured the world a few years ago, Iâd been unpacking this Nordic mindset around wellness and lifestyle in my storytelling for years. I would go on to write an international bestseller, Lagom, with over 15 foreign editions. From Swedish massages to Finnish saunas, the region is synonymous with wellbeing. While Denmark gave the world hygge (intentional presence), Norway friluftsliv (open-air living), FinlandÂ sisuÂ (grit), and Iceland birthed âViking wellnessâ with hot baths and cold dips, the reality is that all Nordic cultures share these values under different names. What makes lifestyle trends from the region particularly appealing globally is the foundations on which theyâre built. From sustainability-focused mindsets and a return to simplicity to curb undue stress, to government-sanctioned free access to nature (think AllemansrÃ¤tten in Sweden), which fosters symbiotic relationships with the outdoors, and overall accessibility for everyone because they are egalitarian countries. The Nordic communal goal is a focus on holistic well-being that can be sustained over the long term by every individual, from professional athletes in their prime to elders. The latest Nordic wellness trend, however, has rather practical origins. Ever wonder how cross-country skiers train when thereâs no snow? Introducing Nordic walking; not to be confused with hiking with trekking poles. According to its governing body, theÂ International Nordic Walking Federation (INWA), which was founded in 2000, Nordic walking is now practised in over 40 countries for health, fitness, recreation, social connection, and competitive sport. As early as the 1930s, competitive cross-country skiers used poles with running shoes for summer training. But it was physical education (PE) teacher Leena JÃ¤Ã¤skelÃ¤inen who brought the concept to the general public in 1966, making it the first documented use of ski poles outside competitive training. âI started Nordic walking in 1998 because it is a fun, social and efficient form of physical activity,â shares Aki Karihtala, president of INWA. âIt takes people back to nature.â At the time, he headed the Sports division at Finnish Sporting goods company Exel, the world's largest cross-country ski pole manufacturer. It was Karihtala himself, alongside his team at Exel, who coined the term Nordic walking, which has been widely adopted âregardless of age, religion and culture, because there are no boundaries,â notes Karihtala, highlighting its accessibility. In 1997, Exel designed the first Nordic WalkerÂ® poles specifically for the activity. A year later, over 500,000 Finns, in a population of roughly five million at the time, had tried Nordic walking. It's said to be especially effective because it engages the whole body while reducing pressure on your knees with ergonomically designed poles. The federation developed its progressive INWA 10 Step Methodâ¢ to teach people the simple technique safely and effectively. Finnish trend and branding expert Katja Presnal is a newer convert to Nordic walking. âIâve studied trends for over 20 years,â shares Presnal. Her personal lifestyle digital platform was read by over 100,000 monthly readers and millions annually. The irony of Nordic wellness being the hottest lifestyle trend at the moment isnât lost on Presnal, who grew up in the Turku archipelago surrounded by bays and lush forests. According to Presnal, after two decades of travelling, she stopped âpreaching trendsâ and started âwalking the walkâ by purchasing a 100-year-old former dairy tucked away in the Finnish countryside for a slower, more intentional way of life surrounded by nature, lakes, and walking trails. âIt was about making everyday life a wellness regimen and creating my own 365-day retreat,â adds Presnal, noting that these were the type of slow living wellness experiences her family would seek in places like Tuscany while travelling. âSo I have, in essence, returned to my Nordic wellness roots, which in hindsight was the richness of my childhood.â The low-threshold accessibility, from a physical and financial standpoint, is what makes Nordic Walking perfect right now for newbies like Presnal. Another benefit Presnal notes is connectivity with people. âPeople are now discovering Nordic lifestyles,â explains Presnal. âYou don't recognise your Nordic way of living as something special that could become a global trend or could be taught and shared with somebody because it's just a part of who you are.â You donât have to wait for the annual World Nordic Walking Day held every May. You can start by: - Finding a local event hosted by over 13 country associations from the Nordics and Baltics to Croatia, Japan, and Australia and joining a group walk with an INWA instructor. - Choosing your favourite local trail and walking at your own pace. - Trying one of INWAâs 25 Nordic Walking Ideas, from themed walks to charity challenges. A version of this story originally appeared on CondÃ© Nast Traveller UK.

item.title: REPORTING: American Airlines baggage fees and how to avoid paying them
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
American Airlines charges checked baggage fees on many flights, but the total price you'll pay depends on many factors, including destination, elite status or whether you carry one of the American Airlines credit cards. If you’re flying with American soon, it’s worth studying up to ensure you're not faced with unexpected charges — or, worse, unable to check your luggage at all. This guide will cover all the information you need to know about American's baggage policy and how you might be able to save money by not paying any fees at all. All passengers are entitled to bring a full-size carry-on bag and a personal item onto every flight, even customers who booked an American Airlines basic economy fare. According to American, a personal item should be no larger than 18 inches by 14 inches by 8 inches and should fit under the seat in front of a passenger. Examples of personal items are backpacks, purses, briefcases, laptop bags and approved pet carriers. The maximum size of a carry-on bag allowed on an American Airlines flight is 22 inches by 14 inches by 9 inches. All carry-on luggage must fit in the sizers available at the airport and/or in the overhead bin or under your seat. Soft-sided garment bags, up to 51 inches, are also allowed as carry-on items. If you’re flying on a domestic, transatlantic or transpacific American Airlines-operated flight, you can check up to 10 bags (with fees attached, explained below). Those traveling through Mexico, the Caribbean, Central America and South America can check up to five bags, though possibly with some seasonal or route restrictions. Overall, American Airlines' checked bag fees vary according to several factors, which include: - Whether you hold a cobranded credit card American Airlines domestic and short-haul international baggage fees For domestic flights (including to Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands) and flights to Canada, Mexico, the Caribbean (except Cuba and Haiti), Central America (except Panama) and Guyana, American Airlines charges the following checked bag fees: - First bag purchased online: $50 for basic economy passengers; $45 for main cabin passengers - First bag purchased at the airport: $55 for basic economy passengers; $50 for main cabin passengers - Second bag purchased online: $60 for basic economy passengers; $55 for main cabin passengers - Second bag purchased at the airport: $65 for basic economy passengers; $60 for main cabin passengers Checked bag fees may vary depending on when you purchased your ticket. American Airlines long-haul international baggage fees American Airlines' checked baggage fees also vary on longer international flights, although many tickets include at least one free checked bag. For transatlantic flights, American Airlines charges the following checked bag fees: - First bag: Free for main cabin passengers; $85 for basic economy passengers For transpacific flights, passengers in both main cabin and basic economy receive their first checked bag for free. A second bag costs $100, while third and additional bags cost $200 each. For flights to and from South America (except Guyana and Venezuela), baggage fees are as follows: - First bag: Free for main cabin passengers; $70 for basic economy passengers American Airlines' overweight and oversized bag fees In addition to baggage fees, American Airlines charges a fee for large bags. If your checked bag exceeds the carrier's standard weight limit of 50 pounds or size limit of 62 linear inches (length plus width plus height), you may have to pay additional fees. The fees are as follows: Note: If a bag is both overweight and oversized, American charges only the higher of the two applicable fees (in addition to any standard checked bag fee). On an American flight, you cannot check a bag that measures more than 115 linear inches or weighs more than 100 pounds. Some destinations have stricter weight restrictions, and fees vary by route. See the cost breakdown in more detail on the airline website. Traveling with sports equipment on American Airlines Skis, snowboards and many other items can count as checked bags as long as they meet the overall size and weight requirements. American Airlines maintains an extensive list of items that you can check. For the most part, there are no additional fees beyond standard checked-bag fees, though overweight charges may apply. However, scuba tanks and windsurfing equipment incur separate fees regardless of any free checked bag allowances. For scuba tanks, the fee is $150 for equipment weighing up to 70 pounds. For windsurfing equipment, you'll pay $150 for every two pieces weighing up to 70 pounds. American does not accept javelins, vaulting poles, or hang gliders as checked items. The maximum size for sports equipment is generally 115 linear inches (length plus width plus height), with a maximum weight of 100 pounds. For travel from Spain's Adolfo Suarez Madrid-Barajas Airport (MAD), the maximum length of any side of a checked item cannot exceed 43 inches. How to avoid American Airlines baggage fees Thankfully, there are several options if you want to avoid paying American's checked baggage fees. Carry an eligible American Airlines credit card Certain Citi / AAdvantage credit cards offer a free first checked bag on eligible domestic American Airlines-operated flights. The premium Citi® / AAdvantage® Executive World Legend Mastercard® (see ) provides a free first checked bag for the cardholder and up to eight traveling companions on the same reservation. Citi® / AAdvantage® Globe™ Mastercard® (see ) offers the same baggage benefit. The Citi® / AAdvantage® Platinum Select® World Elite Mastercard® (see ) offers a free first checked bag for the cardholder and up to four traveling companions on the same reservation. The Citi® / AAdvantage Business™ World Elite Mastercard® (see ) offers the same baggage benefit to the primary cardholder. Keep in mind that free checked-bag allowances from credit cards and elite status cannot be combined. For example, an AAdvantage Platinum member who also holds the Citi / AAdvantage Platinum Select card is entitled to two free checked bags, not three. Take advantage of elite status allowances All four elite status tiers in American Airlines’ AAdvantage program offer checked bag benefits. Up to eight passengers traveling with the elite-status member on the same reservation also receive the same perk. - AAdvantage Gold (Oneworld Ruby): Members receive a first checked bag free on itineraries marketed and operated by American Airlines. - AAdvantage Platinum (Oneworld Sapphire): Members receive a first and second checked bag free on itineraries marketed and operated by American Airlines. They also receive priority baggage handling. - AAdvantage Platinum Pro (Oneworld Emerald): Members receive a first, second and third checked bag free on itineraries marketed and operated by American Airlines. They also receive priority baggage handling. - AAdvantage Executive Platinum (Oneworld Emerald): Members receive a first, second and third checked bag free on itineraries marketed and operated by American Airlines. They also receive priority baggage handling. Additional checked bags are charged at the applicable rate for each bag, rather than starting with the first-bag fee. For example, if you have AAdvantage Gold status and are flying domestically within the U.S., you'd pay $55 online or $60 at the airport to check a second bag, rather than the $45 or $50 first-bag fee for main cabin passengers. Passengers flying on premium fares receive an increased baggage allowance. Domestic first-class customers, business-class flyers and premium economy flyers can each check two bags for free. Flagship First and Flagship Business Plus customers can check up to three bags for free. Several travel rewards cards offer annual statement credits that can help offset checked baggage fees. For example, the Chase Sapphire Reserve® (see ) offers a $300 annual travel credit that can be used toward eligible travel purchases, including airline baggage fees. Meanwhile, the American Express Platinum Card® offers up to $200 in annual airline fee credits for eligible incidental charges, including checked baggage fees. Enrollment is required, and you must select American Airlines as your qualifying airline to receive statement credits for eligible baggage charges. American Airlines offers at least one free checked bag on many international flights, including on main cabin tickets to Europe, Asia, Australia, New Zealand and South America. Basic economy passengers can also check their first bag for free on flights to Asia, Australia and New Zealand, as well as India and Qatar. Check American's baggage policy for destination-specific allowances and restrictions. American Airlines' checked baggage fees vary by destination and fare type, but there are several ways to avoid paying them. Travelers with eligible AAdvantage credit cards, elite status or premium cabin tickets may qualify for one or more free checked bags. Regardless of your ticket type, American also allows all passengers to bring one full-size carry-on bag and one personal item at no additional cost.

item.title: PROFILE: In Lofoten, Norway, a Table Is Set Between Peaks and Fjords
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
âNow you know what itâs like to be in the eye of a storm,â said our hiking guide, Audun Rasmussen, with a grin. I tried to nod, but the wind whipped it into a wobble. We were nearly 2,000 feet up a steep, multi-edged mountain face, and simultaneously getting pelted by rain. If views over picturesque towns and freshwater lakes below are what is typically promised in this part of Northern Norway, today thereâd be none. Instead, fog clung to every nook and crevice of the glacial hulks surrounding us. There was a sense of achievement, certainly. Rain had turned much of our trails into sinking mud, and rock faces to gripless stone. We had used our hands to push past birch and skidded on moss. And we would still have to make our way back down. But for now, we were in the clouds, hiding under rocky overhangs and finding reprieve in reindeer-meat sandwiches, dry fish bites, and chocolate-covered wafers called Kvikk Lunsj that translate to âa quick lunch." Itâs ascents like these, over rock foundations that vastly predate the Jurassic period, that draw close to a million visitors each year to Lofoten Islands. The tiny Norwegian archipelago, 68 degrees north of the Arctic Circle and two flights from Oslo, is a distinctive and dramatic landscape with spiky mountains rising from the Norwegian Sea and sandy beaches fringed by fjords. In summer, buoyed by endless daylight, adventurers arrive from Norwayâs mainland to camp, climb, and swim. But summer was past its twilight when I arrived in late September, and I had come to discover an entirely different side of Lofoten: one found not on its peaks, but on its plates. In a wind-whipped corner of SÃ¸rvÃ¥gen, a village in the southwestern reaches of the archipelago, a cluster of mustard-colored cabins on stilts juts out into the sea. Once home to a cod factory, these buildings have been transformed into Holmen Lofoten, a unique culinary destination and hotel that has welcomed food lovers and adventurers from around the world since 2007. The traditional fishing cabins, known as rorbuer in Norwegian, are distinguished by their corrugated roofs, some of which are topped with insulating grass. Walkways connect the buildings to each other and to wooden decks facing the sea. Inside the guest rooms, large picture windows frame the shoreline. With its simple local furnishings and hand-hewn charm, everything about this place feels elemental. During my four-day stay, Holmen would play host to Kitchen on the Edge of the World, an extraordinary culinary adventure launched in 2018 that welcomes acclaimed chefs into its kitchen four times a year, and brings guests around the tableâand out into the surrounding wild. This, the 30th edition, would be helmed by Matt Orlando, a California-born, Copenhagen-based chef who has worked at some of the worldâs most influential kitchens like The Fat Duck in London and Per Se in New York. For our part, we would feast and drink to our heartsâ content, with the landscape that nurtures every dish spread out just beyond the windows. Ingunn Rasmussen, the warm, chatty matriarch behind Kitchen on the Edge (and hiking guide Audun's sister), took over the property in October 2001 and now runs it with her son, HÃ¥var Holmen. âI wanted to build a space that felt like home, where we could all log off and reconnect with our natural roots,â she said when she picked me up from the airport. A fisherman's daughter, she grew up around this very siteâin fact, one of the cabins still bears her sisterâs childhood scribbles on the wall. After a period abroad, Ingunn returned determined to breathe life back into this corner of Lofoten. What followed was a meticulous restoration focused on preserving the original structures and historical details, and eventually, the addition of a couple of new buildings in the same vernacular to accommodate larger suites. On the first night of the multi-day event, we gathered in the living room above the kitchen. Like all of Holmenâs shared spaces, it is defined by rustic interiors, exposed beams, and raw, sculptural elementsâforaged flora, taxidermy, found objectsâthat echo the weathered landscape outside. That eveningâs dinner would be helmed by Holmenâs own chefs, a young and talented assemblage from as far as Sicily and PiauÃ, in the northeast of Brazil. Trays circulated with shrimp croustades and cocktails that looked like Negronis but told a more local story: the vermouth was infused with foraged blackcurrant leaves, and the Campari steeped with dried berries and yarrow flowers. Each sip seemed to capture the autumnal palette Iâd seen blanketing the hillside on our drive in. The nonalcoholic version was just as heady: an elderflower tonic with a syrup made from freshly picked wild hops from nearby. âHolmen was created because we want to show our guests the Lofoten Islands,â said Ingunn. âAnd food is a critical part of understanding it.â I wandered over to Mia Hjorth Hansen, co-owner of Gedulgt, a cocktail bar in Aarhus, Denmark, and resident mixologist at Kitchen on the Edge. Shelves around her workstation held glass jars filled with foraged and dried ingredientsâcornflower, dandelion, and fireweedâthat she was transforming into elixirs. While visiting chefs rarely return, Hansen is an exception: this is her twelfth Kitchen on the Edge. Still, there's been a through-line among the chefs. Whether Ana RoÅ¡, the renowned Slovenian chef behind the three-Michelin-starred HiÅ¡a Franko, or Simon Rogan, the UK pioneer of the farm-to-table movement, each has shared a commitment to land stewardship. âWe take time picking them,â says Ingunn, âbecause we want [chefs] who will be considerate about the people and wildlife that make this [our] home.â The first night of the event is always designed to be an icebreaker, and Ingunn warned us weâd be surprised by how quickly weâd grow comfortable sharing close quarters over the four days. We were a motley crew, including a geologist from Brunei, a committed adventurer from Dubai, and a Melbourne retiree who travels for intimate food events like this one. Our conversations followed us outside for dessert, onto a deck where we savored ice cream made with black currant leaves and lovage, topped with mascarpone made from Lofoten cream and finished with a meringue charred over binchotan, a Japanese white charcoal. A tracking app suggested the Northern Lights were tantalizingly close, and Holmen kept watch on the skies. It was a taste of what was to come: an intimate experience shaped by live-fire cooking and an embrace of the Arctic elements. The next morning, encouraged by Ingunn's invitation to explore every corner of the property, I wandered into the kitchen to watch Orlando and his sous chef, Tom Siebeler, prepare for their first dinner. âAnything that comes out of that wood-fired oven is going to taste amazing,â Orlando told me, working his way through a pile of reindeer ribs from a sustainable farm run by SÃ¡mi herders just north of Lofoten. Originally expecting chops, he was improvising garnishes to suit the ribs. Reindeer is one of many ingredients Holmen takes care to source locally, alongside cheeses, Lofotlam (a Geographical Indication-protected local lamb), and vegetables. âFor us, knowing where things come from matters, even with the objects we use," Ingunn said. The exquisite tableware we were dining on, for instance, was made by local ceramicist Gunvor Tangrand, whose organic forms pay homage to the surroundings and textured surfaces incorporate old fishing yarn. Orlando had arrived in Lofoten a few days prior with a case full of his favorite building blocksâbarley, Danish yellow peas, several kinds of misoâbut was most excited to work with what he could find in the immediate surroundings. He invited me to step outside to forage for his dinner menu, and we returned with chickweed, corn shoots, and sheep sorrel. âI love cooking in remote places,â he said. âThinking on the fly and exploring the potential in things youâve never worked with is where the coolest ideas come from.â Orlando, like Ingunn, is a bit of a visionary. Some years ago, he opened Amass, a circular restaurant in Copenhagenâs industrial RefshaleÃ¸en neighborhood, where friendly service and an approachable, low-waste tasting menu were paired with a harborside produce garden diners could wander through. Amass has since closed, but last year, Orlando opened Esse in a restored Nordhavn warehouse, and it received its first Michelin star just a few months later. Signature dishes, including his fermented potato bread, made the move, along with his commitment to environmental responsibility. At Holmen, that philosophy is a natural fit. Later that night, as we gathered around communal tables adorned with wildflowers and candlelight, we squealed with delight when the potato bread arrived with allium butter, then again for the fishbone noodles, a masterful creation made by pressure-cooking fish bones and purÃ©eing them until smooth. The collagen-rich mixture gives the noodles their slippery texture, which Orlando complements with smoked chili, sunflower-seed miso, and fermented chili cream. Served family-style, the meal was messy and fun, with utensils set aside so we could savor the main course, the reindeer, with our hands. As a pescatarian, I happily dug into my dish: hedgehog mushrooms grilled with chili-strawberry barbecue sauce and served with Lofoten chimichurri. Outside, the harvest moon kept watch. The weather changes quickly in the North. Quiet and calm one minute, then wild and Baroque the next. âFour seasons in an hour,â joked Holmen. Itâs this unique confluence of climatic conditions that makes Lofoten such a productive landscape: the interaction between the warmer Gulf Stream and cold Arctic waters supports marine life; the long hours of sunlight send plants into hyperdrive; and the sea spray nourishes lamb grazing pastures. âThis land and sea have nourished us for generations,â says Ingunn, who leads guests on foraging walks, returning with fireweed flowers for immune-boosting tea, cloudberries for jam, or lovage for a vibrant, savory butter. But to really understand this landscape is to understand its enduring connection to one particular food source: skrei, or Arctic cod. Here, tepee-style wooden drying racks known as hjeller are as much a visual fixture as Lofotenâs mountains; their distinctive frames have dotted the terrain for more than a thousand years. The racks are empty when I visit, but come January they will be stacked with skrei that have been caught at the end of their annual migration, from the Barents Sea to Lofotenâs milder waters where they spawn. Transformed into tÃ¸rrfisk (wind-dried stockfish), this seasonal bounty has sustained the local economy for centuries. However, like many other coastal societies shaped by the migration and economics of Atlantic cod, Lofoten has been no stranger to ecosystem pressures over the decades, from shifting migration patterns to offshore fishing fleets. Perhaps, it is no surprise then, that a more diversified agricultural movement is taking root. One rainy afternoon, I departed from the cozy confines of Holmen and drove an hour north to the fishing village of Napp, home to Lofoten Seaweed Company, whose products supply Holmenâs kitchensâand line our bathroom shelves. Co-founded by Angelita Eriksen and Tamara Singer, this entirely women-led team dons their wetsuits and hand-harvests seven types of local seaweed, including sugar kelp and nori, from the strong tidal currents of straits like Nappstraumen, transforming them into prized seasonings, even toiletries. Singer showed us around the processing facility inside a traditional rorbu, where Eriksen once cut out cod tonguesâ"a common way for kids in this region to make a bit of pocket money," Singer explainedâand where they now sort, store, and age seaweed for top kitchens like Noma and Geranium in Copenhagen. Theyâre not the only ones. Across the islands, artisanal cheesemakers and farmers growing root vegetables and edible flowers are cultivating the regionâs rich ecosystem. Back at Holmen, I spoke with local BjÃ¸rg-Elin KÃ¤rn, who specializes in food and agriculture systems at Love Food, an organization that connects small-scale producers with local restaurants. âLamb, stockfish, and seaweed are all remarkably sustainable ways of producing food,â she said. âBut conservation only works when the people living on the land and by the sea can make a good living. When a restaurant chooses these products, it helps keep that whole system alive.â KÃ¤rn also works to steer tourism toward local food and agriculture, rather than simply encouraging visitors to âhitch tents and climb mountains.â We talked about the growing toll of [the wrong kind of] mountain tourismâa sore point among residents. Holmenâs own mountaineering guide Audun prefers not to share the names or locations of ascents anymore. He fears that overexposure on social media will draw the wrong kind of attention, not least from underprepared climbers who underestimate both the difficulty of the routes and the whims of the weather. A few years ago, Lofoten banned wild camping, restricting campers to designated grounds. It is clear that tourism has come knocking on Lofotenâs door. In 2025, inbound visitor growth in Northern Norway as a whole, and Lofoten in particular, outpaced the rest of the country, bringing with it a familiar tension: how to welcome visitors while protecting what makes a place worth visiting in the first place. âOur hope is that people come to Lofoten for the right reasons,â Ingunn told me. âUltimately, that will be what helps us protect the islands and our way of life.â Food, increasingly an anchor to how people travel, offers a way to bridge that gap, inviting visitors in while helping them understand the place theyâve come to experience. âHere, you canât separate food production and landscape,â said KÃ¤rn. âMuch of what visitors come to see, whether they know it or not, is shaped by food.â In this way, Kitchen on the Edge hopes to sound a call for travelers to rethink why and how they visit places like Lofoten. Hospitality that takes guests beyond the plate and into the fields isnât a new concept, but here itâs more than a perk: itâs a way of life. One morning, when the weather cleared just enough, we piled into inflatable boats that cut through choppy waters over to an uninhabited island. Once a thriving fishing village, the island was abandoned when motorboats became commonplace in the mid-20th century, and fishing communities no longer needed to live close to spawning grounds. Today, nature has reclaimed this idyllic spotâwhere Ingunn spent childhood summer days picking berries and swimmingâwith waterfalls and carpets of reindeer moss. While others traced the shore on foot, I sat by the jetty and took it all in: the mountains disappearing into the sea, the pair of white-tailed eagles circling overhead, the tiny berries and subarctic flora underfoot. Thereâs something that happens to your brain when youâre constantly zooming out to take in the big picture, then narrowing your focus to the smallest details. I later learned thereâs a name for it: attentional elasticity, a psychological framework that helps you anchor yourself in the present moment. It might be why I felt such a stillness, despite the fog of jet lag and the pull of the action around me. The hotel crew built a campfire around which we ate fish soup, taking turns making pinnebrÃ¸d by winding dough around birch sticks and cooking it over the flames. A flask of aquavitâholy water around these partsâmade an appearance. At Holmen, encounters with nature became part of the daily rhythm. We foraged not just for food but for art, too, gathering moss, mushrooms, and branches heavy with berries to create wild tablescapes with Becky Hindley, a British botanical artist. In a woodworking cabin into which the sunlight poked through optimistically, we spent hours with Lee John Phillips, a woodcarver from Wales, fashioning spoons out of local birch. Itâs a particular kind of luxury thatâs rooted in knowing how to build a life from what the land gives you. As in any home, the kitchen here is the heart of the house, so we kept returning to it: to watch chefs pry open Icelandic queen scallops and slice basketfuls of chanterelles and hedgehog mushrooms. Orlando was always within reach, sharing recipes and starting conversations about food systems. Unlike other modern culinary festivals, there was no peeking behind the curtain, because, in fact, there is no curtain. âThis is my dream for a restaurant,â Orlando said on the night of his final presentation, as we savored grilled pollock with chard shishito butter and sipped a remarkable oat milk drink flavored with green cardamom, rose, and spiced apple. âTo be able to have diners weave in and out and chat as I cook.â As it happened, the clear blue skies we were hoping for never showed for the four days I was there. But the astonishing dishes served beside a crackling oven, the easy camaraderie around the dinner table, and the ever-present possibility of the Northern Lights left me more awake to the world than Iâd felt in months. - Kitchen on the Edge of the World books up fast, so reserve your spot early. You can find the 2027 lineup here, which features a varied cast of chefs, including Toni Toivanen of Copenhagen restaurant Barr and Irish chef and photojournalist James Gabriel Martin. Events are centered around the equinoxes and solstices, and last four nights. - Lofoten Seaweed's colorful shops in Napp and HenningsvÃ¦r are a must-visit for anyone interested in the future of food systems. Seaweed is now globally recognized as a superfood that can help tackle food security and climate emissions, and co-founders Angelita and Tamara, who are often around, are great resources to understand what's at stake. There are also complimentary in-store tastings of hand-harvested Arctic seaweed products (including a tea made from wakame, licorice root, and lemongrass) as well as salts and sprinkles to take home. - Lofoten Gardsysteri is a biodynamic, organic dairy farm that aims to make the best possible use of local resources and distinct flavors. With over 144 goats producing 350 liters of milk under their roof and a vegetable farm at the back (that is open to local schoolchildren for food education classes), expect to find the freshest offerings at the farm shop, where you can linger awhile and enjoy a cheese plate while warming up against sheepskin rugs. Whatever you do, leave with some Brunost, or brown cheese, a local specialty. - Aalan GÃ¥rd is a traditional farm renowned for its goatâs milk cheeses. In addition to cheese production, it features a herb garden, farm animals, and a small shop where visitors can explore and sample locally made products. A visit to Aalan GÃ¥rd is also a great family excursion; note that farm experiences are by appointment only. - Technically not in Lofoten, but well worth extending your trip for, Kvitnes Gard is a historic estate in Hadsel, VesterÃ¥len, that operates as a 15-room farm hotel. It is also home to one of Norway's best restaurants, under the same name, and serves as a great example of regenerative farming in the region. Happily, Kvitnes chef Halvar Ellingsen will be joining Kitchen on The Edge in the fall of 2027 from September 30 to November 4âa collab worth bookmarking.

item.title: IDEA: What Is Mirin? Uses, Types, and Best Substitutes
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
If youâve eaten Japanese food, youâve almost certainly tasted mirin. Alongside miso, soy sauce, dashi, and rice vinegar, the sweet rice wine is a staple of Japanese cooking. It brings richness and complexity to stocks, stews, marinades, and sauces, plus a glossy sheen to glazed dishes like teriyaki. Mirin is often described as sweet with subtle umami, but Sonoko Sakai, author of Japanese Home Cooking, prefers the term koku. âKoku is like umami, but it gives not just flavor but aroma; you feel it with your palate, and it gives depth.â But the type of mirin you buy mattersâand the bottle your local supermarket stocks likely wonât deliver the koku Sakai describes. Hon mirin, or âtrueâ mirin, tends to be pricey and hard to find in the US. Hereâs what sets it apart, when itâs worth seeking out, and what to use when you canât find any. What exactly is mirin? Traditional hon mirin is made from just three ingredients: glutinous rice, koji, and shochu (a Japanese distilled spirit often made from rice). During production, enzymes break down the riceâs starches into âsimple sugars, mostly glucose,â explains Hiroko Shimbo, author of The Japanese Kitchen. That gives mirin a distinctive sweetness without added sugar. Shimbo describes that sweetness as more subtle and âelegantâ than table sugar. She explains that glucose is about 70% as sweet as sucrose (the sugar commonly used in cooking), while Sakai notes that mirin has a lower glycemic index than many other sweeteners. Hon mirinâs alcohol content further sets it apart. With an ABV around 14%, itâs about as alcoholic as some sakes and most grape-based wines, though itâs not generally consumed as a beverage. (One exception is o-toso, a traditional spiced mirin-based New Yearâs drink.) Its alcohol content also makes it useful in cooking. âAlcohol denatures proteins,â says Shimbo. âIt helps them firm up slightlyâitâs also hygroscopic, so it helps to retain moisture.â The result is food thatâs tender, juicy, and rich with umami sweetness. For a bottle of the real thing, Sakai recommends Fukuraijun hon mirin, while Shimbo favors Mikawa hon mirin from Sumiya Bunjiro Brewery. Of course, not everyone is using true mirin. Most American home cooks likely have aji-mirin on hand. Translated as âtastes like mirin,â and widely available and inexpensive, aji-mirin is typically made with glucose or corn syrup, water, rice, salt, and alcohol rather than through the lengthy traditional production process.
