Alcohol content varies by brand; Kikkomanâs aji-mirin, for example, contains about 8%. Both Shimbo and Sakai avoid aji-mirin, citing its less nuanced flavor and more intense sweetness. Shimbo also notes that aji-mirinâs lower alcohol content can affect how it performs in cooking. That said, if you canât find anything other than aji-mirin when shopping, don't despair. J. Kenji LÃ³pez-Alt, author of The Food Lab, also admits that aji-mirin doesn't have the same flavor. âNatural fermentation creates all these byproducts that give hon mirin better aroma,â he says. But he also notes that mirin often makes up only a small portion of a dish and is generally cooked alongside other strongly flavored ingredients. While he uses naturally brewed mirin when he can, âI also cook all the time with aji-mirinâitâs not a problem. You'll notice a difference, but even the cheapest stuff is still going to work just fine.â Both mirin and sake are rice wines used in Japanese cooking, but mirin is considerably sweeter. The difference comes down to how theyâre made. Hon mirin is made with mochi gome (sweet or glutinous rice) and shochu, a distilled spirit that creates an alcohol-rich environment while koji enzymes break rice starches into sugars. Sake, by contrast, uses sakamai (sake rice) and relies on yeast to convert sugars into alcohol, leaving it considerably less sweet. Sake is also brewed for drinking, so youâll find a much wider variety of styles and flavor profiles on the market, some of which would be wasted on cooking. Though mirin and rice vinegar are both rice derivatives, they have very little in common. Mirin is sweet, syrupy, and alcoholic, with an umami undercurrent. Rice vinegar is acidic and tart, with little natural sweetness. Their shared origins might tempt you to substitute rice vinegar mixed with sugar for mirin, but Shimbo, Sakai, and LÃ³pez-Alt agree the result would be far too acidic. Save the vinegar for dishes that need tang, not mirinâs rounded sweetness. Whatâs the best substitute for mirin? According to LÃ³pez-Alt, Shimbo, and Sakai, the best substitute for mirin is sake mixed with a sweetener. The two wines share enough characteristics to make this a closer match than most alternatives, though the result wonât have all the complexity of hon mirin. Any sake you have on hand will do, but Shimbo recommends keeping a large bottle of seishu (clear sake) for cooking. Avoid anything labeled âcooking sake,â which may contain added salt that could throw off your dishâs seasoning. LÃ³pez-Alt generally combines two parts sake with one part sugar by volume. Shimbo prefers brown rice syrup, which she finds more closely mimics the sweetness of hon mirin. Both Shimbo and Sakai also offer maple syrup as a worthwhile swap. If you don't have sake or aji-mirin, you can use dry white wine or dry sherry mixed with a sweetener, though neither is an exact substitute. âDry white wine is closer than a sherry,â says LÃ³pez-Alt, but it brings a distinct flavor that can substantially change the finished dish. As he points out, many recipes that call for mirin also call for sake, so you may need to replace both. None of our experts had an alcohol-free alternative they strongly recommended. Some mirin-style seasonings contain less alcohol than hon mirin, and others are alcohol-free, but they arenât interchangeable in every application. Check the label carefully: Aji-mirin can contain alcohol, and shio mirin (salted mirin) isn't necessarily alcohol-free. Cooking can reduce mirinâs alcohol content, but it doesn't guarantee that all the alcohol evaporates. If youâre strictly avoiding alcohol, choose a product explicitly labeled alcohol-free rather than relying on cooking time. Be mindful of added salt, too. Some mirin-style products are salted to make them unpalatable for drinking, so you may need to adjust other sodium sources in your recipe. How should you store mirin? Hon mirin is remarkably shelf-stable thanks to its sugar and alcohol content. Store it tightly sealed in a cool, dark place rather than the refrigerator, where its sugars may crystallize. Storage recommendations for aji-mirin and other mirin-style seasonings vary by product, so check the label for instructions after opening. Combined with soy sauce and sake, mirin makes a silky tare (seasoning base) for ramen or, when reduced until syrupy, a lip-smacking teriyaki sauce. Try it on salmon, steak, vegetables, and more. Mirin is equally at home in quick-cooking dishes like stir-fried udon with pork and soboro don, as well as slow braises, soups, and marinades. Its delicate sweetness complements fish and tofu, as in brothy steamed bass, and balances the tang of this versatile miso-turmeric dressing. Mirin can also be used in many applications where Western-trained cooks might reach for table sugar. âWhen you use real mirin,â says Shimbo, âthere are many good effects.â

item.title: PROFILE: What Does the PCT Sound Like? Meet the Thru-Hiker Who Recorded His Journey.
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine
On any hike, it’s natural to pause, close your eyes, and listen to the breeze through the trees, the lap of water against a lakeshore, the call of a bird. During his 2023 thru-hike of the Pacific Crest Trail, Tom Kelly stopped to listen, too—perhaps more often than most. While some hikers document their journeys in journals, blogs, or photographs, Kelly, a 41-year-old Angeleno, captured the sounds around him using a couple of microphones and handheld recorders. Two years of editing later, those recordings now comprise a free, publicly accessible sound map representing 200 points along the PCT, offering listeners a chance to experience the trail through its soundscapes. In the very first audio file titled “la posta creek cliff swallows,” you can hear the birds chitter as cars drive by. In another titled “insects at dusk,” chirping bugs pierce the night. Frogs, crickets, bees, quails, rushing water, and rustling grass make up some other sound moments in the files. Each entry comes with Kelly’s field notes, including the recording gear he used, his observations, and even what he experienced in that place. For a nearly six-minute clip of intense wind, blowing sand, and fellow hikers walking by on the edge of the San Gorgonio Pass Wind Farm in California’s Coachella Valley, which he reached in May 2023, he wrote: “finally got to the windfarm and recording a pct landmark. sitting in the colorado desert having just descended from the snowy san jacintos. it is hot, windy, exposed, and i’m getting absolutely sandblasted. hikers passing by as i record the ominous drones of the palm springs windfarm.” And another titled “great-horned owl” captures the call of the elusive bird. Recorded in October 2023 in Northern California’s Plumas National Forest, Kelly wrote: “maybe my favorite recording of the trek. i ended the recording just before the male showed up due to core temp concerns. an incredibly tender dialog ensued between the two of them. i’ll never forget just how excited the female was when the male showed up. heartbreakingly beautiful. a nat geo moment.” Kelly’s attentiveness to sound began in childhood in Wisconsin; he recalls sitting in a sandbox in his parents’ backyard, listening to mourning doves one late afternoon. Music was an early fascination, too. Around the same age, he experimented with the weird sounds of a toy keytar. He went on to study music composition at Columbia College Chicago and continued making music. On a trip to Istanbul, he brought an audio recorder along for the first time, using it to document his travels. “I was like, this could be cool because I can immerse myself in these spaces in a way that you can’t with photography or taking videos on your phone,” he says. “You can close your eyes, put on a soundscape, and kind of be transported back there.” After graduating the music composition program in 2018, Kelly was ready for some extended time outside, away from a studio and desk. He completed his first three- to four-day backpacking trip on Minnesota’s Superior Hiking Trail. Then a 2019 visit to Yosemite unlocked a dream to hike the PCT, and he obtained a permit for 2020. The pandemic derailed his plans. Instead, he explored Idaho’s Sawtooth Mountains and thru-hiked the Superior Hiking Trail over three weeks, carrying an audio recorder on both trips. After a year spent working mostly indoors in 2022, he reached a breaking point, quit his job, and set out to hike the PCT in 2023. Packing along a recorder was inevitable. Kelly didn’t know what shape his recordings would take in the end. His only intentions were to document the PCT’s most natural soundscapes, free of human noise—a priority for soundscape conservationists who see natural silence as an increasingly scarce resource. But even in remote areas, planes, cars, and other people were often audible, making pristine recordings difficult to capture. “I quickly realized that even though you’re on the Pacific Crest Trail in these very remote places, there’s a lot of human presence within earshot everywhere,” Kelly says. “There are so many airports along the West Coast that it becomes a logistical nightmare to try and really significantly alter how you’re traveling in order to record natural soundscapes.” Finding quiet was only part of the challenge. Stopping to record and then getting started again would disrupt the rhythm of the long-distance hike. Any longer than 30 minutes and Kelly’s body would go into recovery mode. Some days, he’d hike through interesting sound moments if he wanted to make up miles. Other times he’d stop to record only to come away with nothing. The equipment he carried also evolved along the way. Two breaks from the trail allowed him to reevaluate his setup. He started out with a Sony a10 handheld recorder and small LOM mikroUsi microphones. His final load out was a high-quality microphone with a makeshift windshield and Zoom F3 field recorder, which he carried in a Cotopaxi 1.5L hip pack. In the end, the 200 recordings included in Kelly’s map—pared down from 350 recordings, totaling about 50 hours—is a combination of pristine nature soundscapes and clips with obvious human presence, such as the wind farm outside Tehachapi, California. The resulting body of work balances soundscape conservation with a broader portrait of the trail, offering every kind of listener something beyond an idealized version of wilderness. “I just want to create a nice experience, and there’s something for everybody in there,” he says. For Kelly, the project was a way to take himself out of the picture—literally, but also as a break from a culture that often makes experiences about documenting the self. The months spent recording nature became both “political resistance” and “personal therapy.” The deeper he got into the hike, he says, the more he synced up with nature’s glacial pace rather than the pace of society. Things got quieter, more spacious, and a bit more minimal as he progressed. Without the usual demands on his attention, he began to notice subtle sounds that might otherwise have faded into the background, like the staccato of a creek or the flutter of leaves. Through this curated sound map, he hopes to share the feeling of being on the trail with people who want to experience it, are living it now, or long to connect back to it. “You don’t even have to put your email address in as a cost,” Kelly says. “There are no cookies. There’s no tracking. It’s just a space for you to show up and explore and create your own playlist of nature sounds if you want.”

item.title: IDEA: 'Wildwood' Is a Love Letter to All Things Portland, Oregon
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favorite films, television shows, and more. This time, we take a look at Wildwood. There are several times when Prue, the 13-year-old protagonist of fantasy epic Wildwood, seems just as in disbelief of the magical world she inhabits as us viewers. As someone who grew up in Portland, Oregon, she thinks she's already encountered the limits of weirdness, and yetâas one of the giant animal denizens of the Impassable Wilderness (known by locals as Wildwood) is quick to remind herâthere she is, speaking with an owl having tea in a waistcoat. Par for the course for the stop-motion studio, Laika's newest creation is a visual feast with soaring eagles the size of commercial airplanes, ancient trees with roots that sprawl across the whole realm, and even an all-out war between worlds reminiscent of the D-Day Landing in Saving Private Ryan. As much as you could lose yourself in these grand spectacles, the film is also emphatic about remembering the magic that imbues just a single blade of grass. As the first Laika movie explicitly set in Portland, the studio looked for inspiration in their own backyards for how to bring the universe of Colin Meloy's titular novel to life. CondÃ© Nast Traveler spoke with Wildwood director Travis Knight on the inspiration behind this exhilarating, stop-motion saga that takes place not too far from home. This movie is such a love letter to Portland, from the Voodoo Doughnuts Prue and Mac eat to the Decembrists posters in her room. This is the first Laika film thatâs been explicitly set where the studio calls home. How did that influence the filmmaking process? It was a joy, unlike anything I've ever experienced. Filmmaking for me is such a privilege to be able to do for a living. To be able to tell a story that was set in the place that I was born, the place that I've lived almost my entire life, the place where our studio is, where so many of us live, was a very special experience because we know that place better than anybody, and we could bring that world to life with real specificity, with real personality. The Portland that you see on screen in Wildwood, while it's a stylized reality because it's animation, very much does represent the truth of what it means to live in that part of the world. One recurring theme in the film is that magic exists in everyday life, in Portland and in the places we least expect. Is the reverse true as wellâin the magical realm of Wildwood, are there fingerprints of Portland and the PNW that the audience can look forward to? There's magic in real life, and there is danger in the fantasy worldâboth of those things are true. I think when you look at Wildwood the place, not the movie, there are places from Portland, the Pacific Northwest, and Oregon, specifically all over it. Crater Lake is in there, Haystack Rock is, and there's all these different, beautiful places of Oregon that we infused into this fantasy land, and that was a great joy. We treated Wildwood the place as if it was an âOregon's greatest hitsâ fantasyland. The idea of treating Oregon on the same plane as some of the great fantasy realms from my youth like Narnia and Oz and Middle Earth was crazy to even think about. It was great to be able to showcase that beauty on the big screen. Thereâs a lot of well-deserved applause for the entirely hand-crafted approach to this film. There's a brilliant blink-and-you-miss-it moment where Prue and Mac pass by an art fair in St. Johns, and a craftsperson selling their wares has a sign at their table saying to get human-made art âbefore it's gone for good.â For this film, did you look to Portlandâs own craft and visual arts culture for inspiration? That's part of the way I look at the world, and it's where our community is from. That particular sign is a visual gag, but it's also something that you would see in Portland. I also think it is a meaningful statement that is relevant to the film and to our culture at large. There is a huge maker community in Portland. It's a group of people that actually celebrates handcrafted things, and that really is what's beating at the heart of the movie, that the film is a celebration of human creativity, of human innovation, of the human touch, and in a world that's often designed to be frictionless, easier, and automated. I think the human touch is something that's special and deserves to be celebrated and deserves to be preserved. Stop motion is such a deliberate practice, where every wrinkle is quite literally sculpted. As a director, are there specific details about a place that you gravitate towards or like to use as launch points? I think when you're approaching a story, you really want to listen to what the story wants to tell you. When I think about Kubo and the Two Strings, I go back to my own experiences when I was exposed to Japan for the first time. I was eight years old with my father, and it was a world unlike anything that I'd ever seen before. It left a huge impact on me, and those were the types of things that I was channeling. When I was making Bumblebee, I thought back to my experience of being exposed to the Transformers cartoons for the very first time. So you start putting these things through your own prism, and with Wildwood, it was very simple because it was the part of the world that I know better than anywhere. Settings, they have their own personality. Ultimately, what is driving all of these things is the theme and the emotion underneath it, and that is the thing that everything else needs to spiral out of. So, in the end, that's really the thing I think about more than anything else: what is the story trying to say, and what is the emotion that we're trying to convey? One of the most circulated facts about the film is the 16-year timeline it took to bring it to life. How did Portland change in that time, and what did your team want to keep sight of when characterizing the city? Portland has changed a lot in 16 years, just like the entire world has changed a lot in 16 years. I first read Colin Molloy's manuscript in 2010. The first movie that we came out with [Coraline] was in 2009, so it was only a year after that that I discovered Wildwood. Portland is a very different place now than it was then. Many, many things have happened since then, some very positive, some tragic. We moved the film into pre-production in 2019, seven years ago. I felt like at the time, we were ready to make Wildwood. Then the whole world turned upside down, and we were hit with a global pandemic the likes of which we had not seen in a century. It changed the whole world, and it changed Portland, and when I see the version of Portland on screen in Wildwood, it's the Portland that I know and the Portland that I love. My hope is that, in time, it can become that again. What were the most challenging sets to construct and animate for Wildwood? Nothing is easy in stop-motion. Everything is difficult in stop motion. But the things that tend to be more manageable are interiors, like a child's bedroom, but even those have so many details that have to be thought of and designed and built and manipulated. What's difficult to do is nature because organic shapes have their own unique grammar. Things like a forest are really difficult to do in stop motion, and I made the decision to set a movie that was almost entirely based in a forest. It's the materials you use, how you build these things, their shape. There's so much beauty to the natural world that's so different and so strange compared to the inorganic world, the things that we humans construct, and most of the film is set in those places. Places like when Prue and Curtis enter Wildwood for the very first time took us a long time to design what that looked like, and it is just so exquisitely gorgeous. It's so beautiful. It took set designers, set dressers, painters, artists, just so many people who built this space to be a work of art. It's something that belongs in a museum, and for a lot of the movie, that moment will pass by within a matter of seconds. What you're seeing is just extraordinary human craftsmanship and artistry on a grand scale, and it's one of the things I love so much about this movie. How did you incorporate the wildlife and ecosystems of the Pacific Northwest into this film? As someone who grew up in the Portland area, I have a lot of knowledge of coyotes. We have a lot of knowledge of crows. We're always next to the natural world. I grew up outside of Portland, essentially on the side of a mountain. I spent most of my childhood days wandering around the forest and climbing up trees and discovering things. The film is emotionally about one primal thing, but there are a lot of layers to the story that we're telling, and part of that is that the film is an eco-fable. That was something that we treated seriously, as itâs something that so many of my collaborators care about deeply, and itâs something I care about deeply. We wanted to try to express that in an organic way without feeling like we were emblazoning it in neon that we're making a message movie. The hope is that you want to honor these things in a way that feels authentic. There's no greater teacher to you than observation, and going out in nature, and seeing how the world was formed, independent of how weâve tried to shape it. Fortunately, in Oregon, one of the many great gifts of the state is that in any direction you go, you will discover it. We poured so much of that into this movie. Now that youâre on the other side of creating a movie based on where you call home, do you have any words to the wise for any creatives out there who feel daunted to tell their own stories about home? What is the piece of advice that they leave out on the old chair-side chest? It was something like writing what you know. I don't think that necessarily means write where you're from, but you have a unique way of looking at the world based on your experiences within it. We know our own lives, unlike anyone else, but that's also the thing that we have to offer that no one else can offer. That's the one thing an artist can do that nobody else can do. They know their own experiences, they own their mind, they know their own imagination, which is different than everybody else's. It's the one thing that we can really offerâhow you've lived, how you grew up, the people you grew up with, the people you've interacted with. Every place has its own unique characteristics and its own unique personality. Even within that, our experiences are different from the person next to us. The daunting thing shouldn't be how to tell a story about your home, it's how to really honor the things that you're feeling, how to honor your imagination in a way that really does it justice. Those are all things that we strive to do as artists. We have big dreams, we have big feelings, and how can we get that out in a way that it makes sense to somebody, and it makes them care?

item.title: REVIEW: I Tested Allover’s All-Season and New Winter Overalls—and I’m Obsessed
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine

This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy I love a Pacific Northwest rugged look—cabin-core, if you will. Some of what I choose is fashion, an expression of how I feel inside and the life I want to live. But I also choose my clothes for durability. Because for me, it’s not just about the look. What I wear has to hold up through the colder months and harsh elements. It has to work on the trails, in the snow, and when I’m brave enough to winter camp. I’ve tried many brands of overalls, and most of them just don’t work for me. I have sensory sensitivities, so certain materials and hardware— buttons, zippers, buckles, clasps–can be a dealbreaker. And then there’s the practical problem I’ve been trying to solve: finding a pair of overalls that I can actually pee in comfortably when I’m on the trail. I was geeked when I came across Allovers, overalls designed for hikers, bikers, climbers, and pretty much any outdoorsperson. They’re casual enough for everyday wear, but built to withstand brutal days in the backcountry. I’ve had my first pair for six months now, and I’m still baffled by how something can be this tough and this comfortable at the same time. Here’s how Allover’s all-season overalls and other gear hold up–and whether the brand’s new winter pair deserves a place in your outdoor wardrobe. I’d planned to test my Allovers, specifically the Women’s Lookout Overalls, on a backpacking trip to Stehekin, Washington, a tiny town at the head of Lake Chelan, tucked into the North Cascades and surrounded by rugged peaks rising more than 9,000 feet. When that trip was cancelled, I had to find another way to put the overalls to the test. So I wore them for months, often on back-to-back days around my property in Eastern Washington–chasing my kids, walking the trails near my home, and letting them get thoroughly rained on. I still haven’t washed them. And somehow, there isn’t a single stain, tear, or hint of smell on them. The overalls are 94 percent recycled polyester and 6 percent spandex. What they feel like: smooth, soft, stretchy, and moisture-resistant. They are BluesignⓇ approved, meaning the overalls have been designed to reduce the environmental and health impacts of textile production. The buckles are one of the reasons I’m obsessed with Allovers. They aren’t cold metal. They don’t unhook or unsnap. They’re nonrelease, with thick, comfortable, adjustable straps that don’t cut into your shoulders at all. Allovers have seven pockets total, the most fun being the hidden pocket in the interior chest (where I put my Beats). And the zippers are hidden within a thick, soft strip of fabric. This has been a sensitivity of mine in the past. I usually feel the zipper through the material, and there’s a stiffness to the material that surrounds it. Not with Allovers. I can’t feel any of the hardware on them. Allovers have a side zipper in just the right spot (about mid-thigh for me) for when you have to use the bathroom outdoors. Other overall brands market such zippers, but I’ve found there usually isn’t enough give and clearance to pee comfortably and cleanly. With the stretchiness of the straps and material, Allovers are so easy to zip down and pull around when nature calls. They can stay on and so can your pack. I have to admit, I use them this way even when I wear them around town. Note: I buy a size up for this reason, to have space for layers and extra flexibility. The Women’s Lookout Overalls, also known as the OG Overalls, are lightweight and work in all four season. They come in four colors: grey, brown, blue, and green, and run from sizes XS to 2X. Mine are a large because I like wearing my pants a bit baggy. I dig a more relaxed, loose fit. After two years of winning over the outdoor community with its Lookout Overalls, Allover announced a winter pair earlier this year. Just like the all-weather pair, Fooses are built for everyday winter life, like a walk in the park with your dog, but are durable for long winter hikes, snowshoeing, Nordic Skiing, hut trips, you name it. I was sent a large pair of Fooses, and though I haven’t winter-tested them yet, I have worn them outside in the middle of the night when the temp was down in the 30s, and been just fine. I slipped off into dreamland under the stars because it felt like I was wearing a comfy sleeping bag. The material is windproof and waterproof, with the same soft interior and incredible amount of stretch. I look forward to wearing them skiing because I know they won’t feel stiff and bulky like other gear. The fit is relaxed and easy, with a wide leg that falls over the ankle for added coverage from cold air and snow. The Fooses feature eight functional pockets including two secure zippered pockets for phone and valuables inside. But something to note: the Fooses run bigger than the Women’s Lookout pair, likely to fit in layers and other gear. If you aren’t an outdoorsy person, and just looking for mountain wear, I’d go a size down from where you’re comfortable for the winterized pair. Since I’m so Allover obsessed, I had to also snag a pair of their Daily Driver Pants. They’re the most comfortable pants I own (and that’s saying something). They’re high rise with plenty of stretch around the hips, with full-length, wide-legs that snap at the bottom if you want to create a cuffs. They run large, so size down from the size you’re comfortable in. I got a medium, since my overalls are a large. Note: If you’re 5’8 or taller, select the long inseam. If you’re shorter than 5’8, select the regular inseam. I took a risk getting the Rope Brim Camp Hat, since I don’t enjoy flat-bills. But this hat surprised me. It’s more flexible than most designed this way, with an adjustable back strap and lightweight ripstop fabric. I love the matcha green color, too. It’s safe to say I’m an Allover junkie. The price may be a bit steep, but for overalls that deliver on style, comfort, and durability, I think they’re worth every penny. I expect these to be a staple in my outdoor wardrobe for years to come. I plan to get plenty of miles out of mine.
